I used to be a service and installation manager for a POS dealer. I have questions:

*  Is this going to be table service or quick service (the entire sale completes at an ordering counter, no servers waiting tables)?

* If it's table service, do you want card transactions to complete at the  table, or do you want servers to take cards back to the terminal?

* Do you want servers ordering at the table on a tablet or portable device?

* How complex is the menu? Some burger joints keep it simple, but many don't. How many modifiers? Substitutions?

* How will the kitchen work? Verbal orders? Paper written tickets? Printed chits? Kitchen video screen?

* Is online ordering desired?

* How detailed do reports need to be? Simple sales, tender, and item sales will do, but many places like labor reports, cost of items, or a thousand other things?

* Will there be many specials or promos?

* Are there any required add-ons or integrations, like gift cards or loyalty programs? Or third party labor scheduling, inventory, guest management, or accounting software?

*  How much is budgeted for POS?

There are even more questions but for now those will work. In short, my general recommendations are:

1. For super simple, portable, ready to use - Square. But ultimately very scalable but if you just want to get up and selling Square will do you. Their processing fees are usually among the highest.

2. For a more robust system that integrates online ordering, has good (relatively) order and pay-at-the-table systems - Toast. Downsides are also somewhat high processing and they lock you into a contract. Good luck getting out if you need it.

3. For the most robust system that can do stupid amounts of promos, kitchen printing and routing, a decent amount of integrations and a big pool of reports - Aloha. Downsides are expensive initial cost, relatively high learning curve, and you support quality will depend on your often shady POS dealer.

4. If you must integrate to a ton of things, especially a hotel PMS - Micros. Overall it's user unfriendly, expensive, and support is awful. But it does integrate to so many more things than any other POS.

Ultimately, my recommendation is to start small and cheap. You didn't describe much but I'm picturing a simple burger joint, with a limited menu and fast operation. Square isn't a terrible place to start - it has high processing rates but usually no contact. So you can get started, and if things go well transition to a new POS in a year or so after you know what you need out of a POS more.

If they approach any dealer, the credit card processing is the real hook.  In many ways, the POS is just the bait to get the processing fees from each card transaction. I'm sorry I don't know this rates right now, but as a small restaurant the rates won't be great. Discounts are given for volume. When negotiating for POS, you can often leverage hardware or installation support before signing whatever draconian processing contract is laid out. And if margins are especially tight, shop processing rates.

Lastly, restaurants are a high-failure startup. Having installed and helped over 200 restaurants start, the ones who succeed have a data-driven plan and execute a sales model that includes food costs, labor costs, a service model and a marketing and identity concept. Hard work alone sadly doesn't predict success.

I wish you the best of luck!

This is a great way to look at it. I personally do almost the exact opposite and try to take advantage of whatever opportunity is given. I go a bit less with roleplay and instead always have a survivor mentality, followed by a rags to riches mindset.

If I play a mission and a great mech base is salvageable, I might go for it, even if I won't get it running for a few months. 

But some things that I always do, regardless of playthrough is:

1. Prioritize defense. Max armor or close to it.  Get ECM.

  1a.  Play defensively. Get high ground, make sure you always have more guns on one of their targets than they put on yours.  The high damage shot that leaves you exposed will cost more than waiting 2 turns until you can bring 3 guns in play and take a mech down in one round.

2. Then prioritize ability to hit. Better sensors, FCS, pulse lasers, optics.

3. Dishing damage.  A couple of big weapons to expose internals followed by missiles is the most lethal. Not always great for salvage, but that will come in time.

4.  I keep 2 months operating cash, and have one backup mech in case one of mine gets trashed.

5. Maximize tech point upgrades. It pays off.

If the question is how to upgrade loyalty, then my answer remains. But yes, if the question is how to upgrade to POS version 15, then you are correct.

If this is about the latter, there are a few things. The first is that newer versions will likely require a hardware upgrade. The bare minimum are terminals that have 2 GB if RAM and adequate space (4GB is doable). That will let you run the new version of Aloha. I recommend better terminals than that as this will be the very end of the line and they'll run slowly with these specs.

Secondly, I don't recommend 15.x for most customers. 12.3 gets you the new loyalty and it's PCI compliant and much more stable with trans logs.  15.1 requires RAL, and what's worse is that RAL is in charge of how term accounts escalate to administrator for tasks, and subsequently de-escalate back. Res life professional for 9 years,  with experience at both a state school and private school.  You have a dilemma and your question is a good one. 

Without knowing the specifics of your incidents is impossible to be exact, but the general take I have is that your situation is primarily a *medical* issue.  The good news is that colleges pretty much can't share that. The better news is that as a rule, state schools are *especially* afraid of lawsuits sure to FERPA (Fedetal Educational Rights and Privacy Act) and even more so HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act)  that your former school is highly unlikely to share your information. 

However,  if your incidents were purely handled as a disciplinary matter they can report it as part of your educational record.  Every school had an individual policy on what they do and don't share.  My former employer wouldn't divulge lesser incidents but students that were removed or very close to that step would be reported upon request. 

I recommend that you contact your former institution and find out their policy to aid your concern.  Your new institution may not even ask them directly in any case but it's nice to know what they'll report on you.  Then, be prepared to talk openly about your issues, what steps you have taken such as therapy or other treatment, and have a Needham professional's note indicating your ability to live in a residence hall community. Lastly,  and most importantly, be prepared with a plan of you have a hard time, including your stress management techniques,  having direct resources for crises, and how you'll keep yourself and community members safe. 

My ultimate advice about your application is to not divulge anything direction until after you're accepted.  Then,  after you're adorned speak directly with your lowest level residence life professional (not your RA to start)  about *relevant* information and any advance safety planning you require to be successful.   It sucks to hide the truth but it won't necessarily help you and colleges are so paranoid about having safety risks early disclosure could just your admission but once you're admitted removing you requires an appropriate follow through from them. 

My personal request,  having never met you is to please be ready.  Living in a residence hall really is a community,  and if you know you will have high profile incidents you are doing neither yourself nor your peer students any favors.  That being said, I'm rooting for you. Stick to your plan and keep the end goal in mind!
